Cyberpunk

The visual look of the cyberpunk science-fiction genre, as designers apply it to posters, games, and interfaces: a near-black night city lit by saturated cyan, magenta, and warning-yellow neon, monospace terminal text, heads-up-display frames and brackets, and glitch interference. The name comes from Bruce Bethke’s 1983 story and the 1980s fiction of William Gibson. Blade Runner (1982) and Akira set its look. This record covers the screen and graphic look. Cybergoth fashion, techwear, and cyberdelic art are related branches.

Dystopian / Gritty / Nocturnal / High-tech / Rebellious / Tense

Visual grammar

  • Neon on black. A near-black, blue-black ground lit by small areas of saturated cyan, magenta, and acid or warning yellow. Envato: “hot pink neon contrasted with the cool metallic blues and grays”.
  • Glow, not shadow. Lines, frames, and letters give off light: blurred halos with no offset, as from neon tubes and screens. There are no drop shadows, because the light source is the object.
  • Terminal and HUD type. Monospace text for data, labels, and body, and condensed or squared sans-serif capitals for display. Labels carry codes, numbers, and status words.
  • Heads-up-display frames. Thin 1 px frames, corner brackets, chamfered corners, tick marks, and numbered panels, as on a targeting screen or a terminal window.
  • Dense data panels. Information sits in many small, labelled panels and tables, like a dashboard or a wall of signs. Diagonal cuts and hazard stripes break the grid.
  • Night city and the cyborg body. Rain-wet streets, megastructures, vertical neon signs, often in Japanese or Chinese, cables, implants, and holograms. Wikipedia names Hong Kong and Kowloon Walled City as models for the city.
  • Glitch and flicker. Color-channel splits, scan lines, flickering neon, and typed-out text. Envato describes the glitch effect as “fallibility” in holograms and displays.

Identity

Name
Name used by designers and vendors
Also called
Cyberpunk design, Neon noir, Tech noir
Era
1982–present. Wikipedia: the Akira manga began in 1982, the year of Blade Runner, and Neuromancer followed in 1984. Envato wrote in 2017 that “cyberpunk is big right now”. The Aesthetics Wiki uses Cyberpunk 2077 (2020) as its lead image. The look continues in games and marketing.
Regions
United States, Japan, Hong Kong, International
Wikidata
Q174526
Name used by
Wikipedia: Cyberpunk, Aesthetics Wiki: Cyberpunk, Envato (5 September 2017): A Cyberpunk Future Is Closer Than You Think

Lineage

  • Influenced by Film noir. Wikipedia: “much of the genre’s atmosphere echoes film noir”. The deep shadows, rain, and hard light of noir carry over into the neon night city.
  • Related to Tech noir. Wikipedia: some cyberpunk films “have been described as tech-noir, a hybrid genre combining neo-noir and science fiction or cyberpunk”.
  • Related to Glitch art. The Aesthetics Wiki lists glitch art as a related aesthetic. Envato names the digital glitch, “the digital flickering caused by interference”, as a cyberpunk effect.
  • Related to Cybergoth. Wikipedia: cybergoth is a fashion and dance subculture that “draws its inspiration from cyberpunk fiction, as well as rave and Gothic subcultures”. It is a fashion branch, not covered here.
  • Related to Synthwave. The Aesthetics Wiki lists synthwave as related. Both use neon on black. Synthwave looks back at 1980s pop culture, and cyberpunk shows a dystopian near future.
  • Related to Vaporwave. The Aesthetics Wiki lists vaporwave as related and says the revival “often blends traditional cyberpunk motifs” with vaporwave and synthwave.
  • Related to Y2K aesthetic. The Aesthetics Wiki lists Y2K Futurism as related. Both are digital futures of the late 20th century, with opposite moods.

Classification rubric

The test for a new reference

Identifies the style

  • The ground is black or near-black blue, and saturated cyan, magenta, or yellow neon lights the elements.
  • Lines and letters glow with a blurred halo that has no offset.
  • Monospace terminal text, codes, and numbered labels appear throughout, with condensed capitals for display.
  • Thin HUD frames, corner brackets, chamfered corners, or hazard stripes structure the content.
  • Night city, cyborg, or screen imagery with glitch artefacts.

Rules it out

  • A pastel sunset, Windows 95 windows, or Greek statues: that is vaporwave.
  • A striped setting sun over a grid horizon with chrome lettering and no dystopian content: that is synthwave.
  • A light silver or white ground with rounded candy-plastic shapes and an optimistic tone: that is Y2K.
  • Soft, rounded, friendly controls on a light ground.
  • Drop shadows that suggest daylight from above.

Often confused with

Vaporwave
Vaporwave is pastel pink, purple, and cyan, ironic and nostalgic, with gray Windows 95 windows and classical statues. Cyberpunk is dark and serious, with saturated neon, terminal text, and HUD frames.
Y2K aesthetic
Y2K is bright, silver, rounded, and optimistic: chrome blobs and candy plastic around the year 2000. Cyberpunk is black, square or chamfered, and dystopian.
Synthwave
Synthwave is retro 1980s nostalgia: a striped sunset over a neon grid horizon, chrome logotypes, and sunset gradients. Cyberpunk has no sunset. It shows a dense night city, HUD panels, terminal text, and glitches.
Glassmorphism
Dark glassmorphism dashboards can use neon accents, but their panels are frosted, translucent, and generously rounded. Cyberpunk panels are opaque, square or chamfered, and outlined with glowing hairlines.
Cybergoth
Cybergoth is a fashion and club subculture: neon falls, goggles, and PVC. This record covers the graphic and interface look, not dress.

Ideas to carry forward

  • Use a near-black, slightly blue background, and keep neon colors to lines, labels, and small fills.
  • Pick two or three neon colors: cyan, magenta, and acid yellow. Give each one a job, for example yellow for primary actions and cyan for frames.
  • Make frames glow with a blurred box shadow that has no offset.
  • Set body text, labels, and data in a monospace font. Set display headings in condensed sans-serif capitals.
  • Frame panels with 1 px lines, corner brackets, and chamfered corners, and number or code them like HUD readouts.
  • Use color-channel offsets, scan lines, or hazard stripes for emphasis, in small areas.

Keep the function

  • Do not round corners or use pill shapes.
  • Do not use drop shadows with an offset. Light comes from the elements themselves.
  • Do not use pastel colors or sunset gradients. They read as vaporwave or synthwave.
  • Do not put long body text in neon colors. Keep it in a pale, cool off-white with a contrast ratio of at least 7:1.
  • Do not add Japanese or Chinese text that you cannot read or check. Use short, correct phrases, or none.
  • Do not animate flicker or glitch continuously. Respect prefers-reduced-motion.

Useful directions: video games and game studios, esports teams and tournaments, electronic music, club nights, and festivals, developer tools, security, and hacking products, science-fiction film, books, and fan sites.

Poor fits:

  • Health, children’s, and wellness products. The style signals danger, surveillance, and decay.
  • Banks, insurance, and government services. Its anti-corporate tone undercuts trust.
  • Long-form reading. Dark grounds, monospace body text, and glow tire the eye over many pages.
